The same code on both phones. It is never sent over the air - it only proves you and your buddy both know it, and it keys the encryption.

A 6-digit code is quick to type but easy to guess for anyone who records your handshake. For a ride where that matters, use words.

Everyone uses the same ride code. The host starts the ride and the others join it; no pairing needed. Needs Google Play services. Riders further apart than one phone\'s range are reached through the riders between them.
Internet ride is on: voice goes over mobile data through your relay. Use a word code.
Nobody has joined yet. Riders appear here as they connect.
SCO audio channel open — voice active.
Start the server, then put the C30 in universal intercom mode and pair.
Waiting for an HF device to connect...
No AT commands yet. Start the AG server and connect a device.
No HF device connected via system HFP.\nPair the C30 in phone mode first.
Uses about 16 MB of mobile data per hour of talking, per rider listening.
Rider positions and distance are not sent on internet rides.

The relay\'s owner can see your phone\'s internet address, when you talk and how much, but not what is said, who you are or where you are. Use a five-word ride code: the relay can test guesses against a short code.
Not a valid address. It must start with wss:// (plain ws:// is not accepted).

For city and plains riding where there is phone signal. Voice goes over mobile data through a relay server you run. It is still encrypted end to end with your ride code, so the relay cannot hear it. It does not work without signal; use Bluetooth, Wi-Fi Direct or a group ride there.
Group rides then use mobile data and the relay instead of Bluetooth and Wi-Fi. Off by default.
Convenient, but Android suspends A2DP while the headset mic is open, so music turns mono and muffled for the whole call.
Android 13+ with an LE Audio headset: mic and high-quality output at once. Few helmet headsets support it yet.
Keeps the headset on A2DP. Usable at town speeds; wind beats it on the highway.
USB-C or 3.5 mm, mounted in the helmet. Best wind rejection, and the headset stays on A2DP so music stays stereo.
Town riding. Takes out the steady hiss and rumble without touching the voice.
Mixed roads. Stronger than Light, still natural; a good default when speeds vary.
Only the wind low-cut and the noise gate. Most natural voice, but your buddy hears the bike.
Highway. Removes engine and wind roar; the voice sounds slightly processed in exchange.
Phones stop apps to save power, and that is the main reason a call ends in the middle of a ride. Do these once.
Bluetooth connects the two phones, and on newer Android the nearby-devices permission also lets the long-range Wi-Fi link work. Pair your buddy\'s phone once in Android\'s Bluetooth settings.
Android did not grant it. You can allow it in the app\'s system settings.
Set a ride code on the start screen, then host or join. You can run this setup again from Settings.
You switched on sharing your position. It is used only to show your buddy how far away you are, goes only over the phone-to-phone link and is never uploaded or stored.
The app needs your microphone to carry your voice to your buddy. Audio is never recorded or stored.
While a call runs the app shows one notification with Mute and Stop. Android needs it to keep the call alive when the screen is off.
Sound would come out of the phone\'s loudspeaker. Connect a headset.
A headset is connected but its microphone is not in use. Connect it in call mode, or the other rider will hear the phone\'s microphone instead.
Nothing to listen through. Connect a headset or speaker.
Looks good: the headset is used for both speaking and listening.
No headset found. Calls will use the phone itself, which is too quiet and noisy on a bike.
A call is running, so the test is unavailable.
Speak for a few seconds. You will see the microphone level, then hear yourself back through the headset. Nothing is sent to anyone or saved.
It was very loud and may distort. Move the microphone a little away, or lower the headset\'s input gain.
The microphone could not be opened. Is another app using it?
I could barely hear you. Check the microphone, or move it closer to your mouth.
Talk to the rider next to you with no internet and no mobile signal. This takes about two minutes: a few permissions, a battery setting that keeps calls alive, and a test call.
No account, no cloud, no tracking. Your voice goes straight from phone to phone, encrypted with your ride code.

If the call does stop, the app posts a notification rather than restarting itself. Android 14 refuses to create a microphone service from the background, and a silent retry is what produces one-way audio. Open the app and tap Start again.
Settings > Battery > App launch > Rider Intercom
Turn off Manage automatically, then enable all three manual options
Settings > Apps > Manage apps > Rider Intercom
Other permissions > allow Display pop-up windows while running in background
In Recents, pull the app card down and tap the padlock so it is not cleared
No vendor-specific battery manager detected on this phone. Standard Android rules apply, so the exemption above should be enough.
Settings > Battery > Battery optimisation > Rider Intercom > Don\'t optimise
Settings > Battery > Advanced > turn off Sleep standby optimisation
In Recents, lock the app card
Settings > Battery > App battery management > Rider Intercom
Turn off Smart control, turn on Allow background running
Settings > Apps > Rider Intercom > Allow auto-launch
Add Rider Intercom to Never sleeping apps
Make sure it is not in Sleeping apps or Deep sleeping apps
Android\'s Doze will suspend the call once the screen has been off for a while. Ask for the exemption here.
Done. This app is already exempt from Doze.
Doze and battery managers are what end rides early
This phone\'s manufacturer overrides standard Android and can kill the call anyway. Work through these once:
Settings > Battery > Background power consumption management
Set Rider Intercom to Allow high background power consumption
i Manager > App manager > Autostart manager > turn Rider Intercom on
%1$s is deafened: they cannot hear you
%1$s is muted: you will not hear them
Bluetooth advertise (so buddies can find you)
Location (needed for Bluetooth on this Android)
Switch off to send your voice with only the wind low-cut and the noise gate.
Lets a buddy on an older version of this app connect without encryption or a ride code check. Anyone nearby could then listen in, and the call screen shows a warning for as long as it lasts.
Auto: choose the strength from my speed

Light in town, Medium on faster roads, Strong on the highway, switching only after the speed has held for about 10 seconds. Needs \"Share my location\" below; until there is a GPS fix it uses the strength you picked, and it keeps its last choice if the fix is lost. Picking a strength yourself turns Auto off.
Warn me when a rider falls behind

A short beep on your own phone (never sent to anyone) when a rider stays farther away than the distance below for the time below, then again every 30 seconds while they are still out. Needs sharing on.
Saves the recent app log without positions, ride codes, names or Bluetooth addresses, and opens the share sheet. Nothing is sent anywhere unless you pick an app.
Lower music when I talk too
Music always lowers while your buddy speaks. Turn this on to lower it while you speak as well.
Off: the intercom takes no audio focus at all, music keeps playing at full volume and the voice is lifted 6 dB instead. Use this if your music app pauses rather than ducking.

A small neural network (RNNoise) that copes better with gusty, uneven noise. It has no strength setting, uses noticeably more of the processor and battery, and adds about 11 ms of delay. If your phone cannot keep up, the app switches back to Standard by itself.
Light on the battery and the processor, with a strength you choose. Good for steady noise such as engine hum and road roar.

Slowly raises your voice when you talk quietly or the mic has slipped, lowers it when you shout, and stops it ever clipping. It changes over a few seconds, never between words, and it leaves silence alone. Off by default.
Lets the headset button run the intercom. What each press does is set under Remote buttons below; a single press is left to your music app unless you change it.
Headsets differ, and some map their main button to the voice assistant, which the app cannot change.
Pure black background and brighter text, for bright sunlight through a visor.
Calibration: start a call, then press your headset button here to see which key code it sends.
Choose the language of the app. Ride-code words stay in English so both phones always match.
Follows the language set in Android
Taller buttons that are easier to hit with gloves on. Text size follows the phone\'s font size setting.
Legacy audio path is on (AudioRecord/AudioTrack instead of Oboe). Long-press the title to switch back. Applies from the next call.
Tones when the link drops and returns
A short falling tone when the connection is lost, a rising one when it comes back. The app keeps trying to reconnect either way.
Precise location was not allowed, so nothing is shared. Allow \"Precise\" location for this app in the phone\'s settings, then switch this on.
The headset mic is the one trap in this design: opening it drops the headset off A2DP and music turns mono for the rest of the ride.
A short local tone, never sent to the other rider, at most one every two seconds.
Beep when you talk over your buddy

This cleans the voice you send, so your buddy hears you instead of your engine. It cannot cancel noise at your own ear the way an aviation headset does — that needs a microphone inside the earcup and a sub-millisecond loop, which is a property of the headset, not the phone.
This phone also offers: %1$s. Those run in hardware and are used automatically when noise cancellation is on.
Tap a row to change what it does. Press-and-hold gestures depend on your headset, so check them with the key code line above.
Calls are encrypted with your ride code. A buddy who has the wrong code, or whose app cannot encrypt, is refused.
Permissions, battery settings and a test call

Shows how far away your buddy or group is, and lets them see how far you are. While this is on, your phone reads its GPS and sends your position straight to the riders in your call, encrypted with your ride code. It goes phone to phone only: there is no server and no internet, nothing is stored, and it stops when the call ends. You see distances only while you share your own. It costs some battery. Off by default.
Cuts twice as sharply below the frequency. More wind removed, slightly more change to the sound near the cutoff.
An open call is the point of this app: the channel is always up and speaking is all it takes. Push-to-talk is there for helmets too noisy for a detector, or riders who would rather hold a button.
Voice-activated. First speaker takes the channel; everyone else is muted until they stop.
The detector never opens the channel. Only the on-screen button, the notification or the headset button do.
Bluetooth, moving to Wi-Fi Direct if it degrades
Start on Wi-Fi Direct: 50-100 m, more battery
%1$s dB over the noise floor, %2$s ms to open
How eagerly the channel opens when you speak. Lower sensitivity at highway speed, higher with a boom mic.
Music stays on the phone\'s media volume. The headset volume rocker moves both together, because the voice plays as media.
Use the volume buttons during a call
While a call is running the volume buttons stop changing the volume and do what is set above instead, and the headset play/pause button is taken by the intercom too. Off by default.
Wi-Fi Direct is not usable right now: %1$s. Auto will stay on Bluetooth until that is fixed.
Wi-Fi Direct is ready on this phone. Auto will move the call onto it if Bluetooth starts losing frames.
Removes the low thump of wind and engine from the voice you send. Raise it if the highway still booms in your buddy\'s ears; lower it if your voice sounds thin.
SOS. Tap twice, or hold for three seconds, to send an alert to your buddy
Switch on \"Share my location\" to see how far away it is.

SOS sent with your last known position. It is repeated twice.

Off by default. It only looks for a new version; it never downloads or installs anything by itself.

The checksum is published next to the file, so it catches a damaged download. The protection against a swapped file is Android\'s signature check.

Android needs you to allow installs from this app first. Switch it on, come back and tap Install again.
Version %1$s is downloaded and its SHA-256 matches. Android will also check that it is signed with the same key as this app before installing.

The app makes no network connections except when you ask it here to look for an update. A check contacts GitHub (api.github.com) over HTTPS and sends nothing about you beyond what any web request carries, such as your IP address.
